newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam's Giap calls for peacetime vigilance.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam's Giap calls for peacetime vigilance.

text.p: Vietnamese war hero General Vo Nguyen Giap on Thursday paid homage to hundreds of veterans who fought French colonialists 50 years ago and warned that the country must be on its guard, even in peacetime.
"Our ideal is independence and socialism," Giap told Reuters after a rousing speech to rows of bemedalled old soldiers at the Soviet-style Viet-Xo palace in central Hanoi.
"We must build the country and always be vigilant," he said.

His address followed a week of elaborate preparations to celebrate the anniversary of a battle between French troops and Viet Minh forces, which began in the streets of Hanoi on December 19, 1946, and raged for 60 days.
Giap rose to fame as one of this century's military geniuses after masterminding the communists' defeat of the French at Dien Bien Phu in 1954.
He is also seen as the architect of the communist military victory over the forces of United States and U.S.-backed Saigon in the Vietnam War which ended 21 years later.
Now 84, still bright-eyed and spritely, the silver-maned general is one of the communist country's most revered figures.

Giap, speaking in French, said Vietnam had drawn lessons from other countries during its decade-old shift from a socialist planned economy to one based on market principles, but stressed that the country's culture must be safeguarded.
"There are a lot of positive changes and we have forged a policy of renovation the Vietnamese way," he said, wagging a finger.
He said the renovation drive, which has included opening doors long closed to the outside world, had also brought corruption, bureaucracy and "social evils".

Hanoi launched a blitz against prostitution, pornography, drug abuse and gambling ahead of a party congress earlier this year and has regularly warned of "peaceful evolution", by which it means back-door subversion of the regime.
Defence Minister General Doan Khue last week issued a rallying cry to the military, warning that "hostile forces" were stepping up their efforts to undermine the country's government.

Khue, who ranks sixth in the elite politburo, said Hanoi had smashed hundreds of plots to sabotage or incite riots and needed to seize the opportunity now to strengthen the military through better equipment, better personnel and increased training.

The streets of Hanoi were decked with red banners celebrating National Resistance Day and dozens of hero veterans, many of them frail and tearful, attended a formal wreath-laying ceremony at the tomb of the "unknown soldiers" who died in Vietnam's wars.
Vietnam often uses the anniversary of military victories as a platform to send a message to the people.
Thursday's Resistance Day anniversary was no different.

"As we enter the new period...we are determined to turn patriotism, self-reliance and internal strength, the revolutionary heroism of resistance against the French to revolutionary heroism in the cause of building and defending the fatherland," the party daily Nhan Dan said in an editorial to mark the event.
"We are determined to defeat backwardness and poverty and carry out...the resolutions of the Eighth Party Congress."
